This lab has exercises that reinforce the section "Working on remote machines" of Lecture 4 (`lectures/lec04_remote_machines_postgres.qmd`) and the sections "Finding and stopping a process" and "Background job administration" of Lecture 2 (`lectures/lec02_linux_advanced.qmd`). Parts 1 and 2 get you onto Moriah, the HUJI cluster, and move files back and forth. In Parts 3 to 7 you run **everything on Moriah**. You will need a second terminal logged into Moriah in a few places.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Ground rules
* Run every command yourself. Many answers depend on what you see (and your PID numbers will not be the same as anyone else's).
* Leave the "#TODO text [question text] text" line and start a new line underneath and write your answers on that new line
* This file stays on your laptop, and you commit and push it from there. Keep it open on your laptop while your terminal is on Moriah.
* Moriah is **shared** and its login machine is used by everyone. Other people's programs will show up in your output, including your classmates' `sleep` commands from this very lab. Only ever touch your own processes. Run nothing heavy on the login machine: everything here just sleeps or prints a line per second.
* Clean up after yourself. Every part ends by stopping the processes it started. Check with `pgrep -u $USER -a sleep` that none are left over.
* **Never** put your private key (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`) in this file or anywhere else.
:::

#TODO [How many cores and how much memory does Moriah's login machine have compared to your laptop? <1pts>]
Moriah’s login machine (moriah-gw-02) has 2 cores and about 11 GiB of RAM (about 7.9 GiB available). My MacBook has [N] cores and [X] GB of RAM, so the laptop is much more powerful than the login machine. That’s by design: the login machine is a small, shared entry point used by many people at once, and the heavy computation on a cluster is meant to run on separate compute nodes, not on the login machine.
#TODO [Why is the `pwd` different on Moriah vs your laptop? <1pts>]
They are two different computers with different operating systems and separate filesystems. On Moriah (Linux), my home directory is /sci/home/ivetta.volowel, and it is tied to my cluster account ivetta.volowel. On my Mac, it is /Users/elivolowelsky, tied to my local account. cd ~ goes to the home directory of whichever machine and user I’m currently on, so the path differs.
#TODO [why can't you just `ssh` straight to `moriah-gw` from home? What is the name for a machine like `bava`? <1pts>]
moriah-gw is inside the university’s internal network and isn’t directly reachable from the open internet (e.g., from home), so I can’t connect to it directly. I first connect to bava, which is reachable from outside, and it forwards me to moriah-gw (that’s what ssh -J does). A machine like bava is called a jump host (also called a bastion host). It is a single, hardened and monitored entry point (protected here by OTP), which means the internal machines don’t need to be exposed publicly.

#TODO [Why was the second `rsync` run so much faster? <2pts>]
The second run was much faster because rsync compares the source with the destination
(by file size and modification time) and only sends files that are missing or changed.
In the first run all the files were new, so all of them were sent. In the second run
nothing had changed, so almost no data had to be transferred, only the file list was compared.

# Part 3: Looking at processes with `ps` and `pgrep`

From here to the end of the lab, everything is done on Moriah (unless it says otherwise):

```bash
#TODO [login to moriah <0pts>]
cd ~/lab04

```

`sleep 600` does nothing for 10 minutes, which makes it a perfect process to look at. The `&` at the end runs it in the **background**, so you get your prompt back. The shell stores the PID of the last background process in the variable `$!`:

```bash
sleep 600 &
echo $!
```

#TODO [what did the line `[1] <number>` that appeared after the first command show, and how is `echo $!` related to it? <1pts>]
[1] is the job number assigned by the shell to this background job, and the number after it is the PID (process ID) of the background process. echo $! prints the PID of the most recently started background process, which is the same number.

```bash
jobs
```

#TODO [Is the output of the above expected? Why/why not? <1pts>]
Yes, it is expected. jobs lists background jobs started in the current shell. We started exactly one, so it shows that single job as Running.

Now let's find this job in the linux process list. `ps` can show just the columns you ask for, for just the processes you ask for. Read the `-o` and `-p` options in `man ps` and run:

```bash
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p $!
#TODO [the parent PID of your `sleep` is the PID of another process. Write the command that shows that process' command, and say what it is <1pts>]
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p <46311>

```

```bash
#TODO [keep following the parents upward, one `ps` at a time, until you find the program which let you into moriah. The user will be "root". <1pts>]
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p 1379316
Output: sshd-session: ivetta.volowel@pts/227
ps -o pid,ppid,user,stat,command -p 1379134
Output: sshd-session: ivetta.volowel [priv] — owned by root. This is the SSH daemon process that let me into Moriah.
```

#TODO [How does this explain why your background job is at risk when the connection drops? <1pts>]
The process tree shows that sleep is a child of zsh, which is a child of sshd. If the SSH connection drops, sshd terminates, which causes zsh to receive a SIGHUP signal and terminate, and zsh sends SIGHUP to all its children (including sleep), killing them too. The entire chain dies from the top down.


# Part 4: A terminal that survives: `tmux`

`tmux` keeps a whole **terminal** alive, so that you can go away and come back to see it as you left it. Start a session called `lab4` on Moriah (if you get `command not found`, look for it with `module spider tmux`, as in the lecture):

```bash
tmux new -s lab4
```

You are now inside tmux (note the green bar at the bottom). We now navigate to the shared folder where there's a program you should run that persists.

```bash
cd /sci/courses/2026/52002/shared/
```

Now run the shared program called `tmux_proof`. Run it with your name as follows.

```bash
./tmux_proof "<first name> <last name>" #fill in your first name and last name!
```

After 24hr it will print out a unique encrypted code. We will decode it to reveal your full name and the hostname of the computer (which should be moriah). So don't share codes as you won't get credit if your name doesn't appear.

Detach: press Ctrl+B, release both keys, then press d. You are back in your normal terminal on Moriah. Then go back into the terminal and ensure it's still running.

```bash
tmux ls
tmux attach -t lab4
```
Detach again: press Ctrl+B, release both keys, then press d.

Now you can skip the next TODO and continue the rest of the assignment. You can exit moriah and come back in 24hr and it will still be running.


```bash
tmux ls
tmux attach -t lab4
#now copy the code
```

#TODO [Look at the deaths column of your answer above. What went wrong? Write the corrected query below, using a condition from the lecture <2pts>]
The deaths column is empty (NULL) for all 5 rows because in Postgres ORDER BY ... DESC places NULL values at the very top before actual numbers. Since Puerto Rico counties have NULL for deaths, they came first. We fix this by filtering out missing values with AND NOT deaths IS NULL.


```sql
#TODO [corrected query <1pts>]
SELECT county, state, deaths FROM covid WHERE date = '2020-11-30' AND NOT deaths IS NULL ORDER BY deaths DESC LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10;
--     county    |    state     | deaths 
-- --------------+--------------+--------
--  Bergen       | New Jersey   |   2124
--  Suffolk      | New York     |   2053
--  Hidalgo      | Texas        |   2050
--  Philadelphia | Pennsylvania |   2026
--  Clark        | Nevada       |   1767
```

#TODO [Why do the two counts differ? <1pts>]
Because LIKE is case-sensitive while ILIKE ignores upper and lower case. In the dataset, "Lake" always starts with a capital "L" (for example, "Lake" or "Salt Lake"), so LIKE '%lake%' with a lowercase "l" finds 0 matches, whereas ILIKE '%lake%' finds all 7.
